newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-ABB first quarter profit tops expectations.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-ABB first quarter profit tops expectations.

text.p: Swiss-Swedish Engineering conglomerate ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG on Tuesday reported an eight percent rise in first quarter profit, exceeding low-key market forecasts.
Goran Lindahl, ABB's new president and chief executive, said he was satisfied with the results, especially a 16 percent rise in new orders which he saw as a promising sign for the future.
"It's a result that we are satisfied with," Lindahl said.
"I would especially underline the order intake. That is promising for the future," Lindahl told Reuters.
Market expectations for ABB's first quarter were restrained, following its 1996 results in February which had disappointed markets and lead to many downgradings and forecast reductions.
The first quarter result, however, was warmly welcomed by analysts, who had anticipated flat profits.
In Zurich shares of ABB's Swiss-quoted parent were up six Swiss francs to 1,754 francs and in Stockholm the shares of ABB's Swedish wing were up 3.50 Swedish crowns to 91 crowns.
ABB's first quarter net profit rose eight percent to $236 million and operating profit rose 11 percent to $472 million.
Adjusting for the strong U.S. dollar, which has a negative effect on ABB's reported results, net profit in local currency terms rose 14 percent and operating profit rose 17 percent.

The second year of economic slowdown in Western Europe continues to dampen demand for many of ABB's industrial and investment goods, while good growth in emerging markets and the favourable effects of cost reduction programmes again benefited results positively.
Lindahl confirmed he still expects 1997 earnings to at least reach 1996's $1.233 billion, but added this outlook was cautious and only set a minimum for the expected profits.
"This is definitely a floor and no ceiling whatsoever," Lindahl said, adding he was confident about this forecast.
Lindahl said the outlook was cautious because ABB was still in the second year of a downturn in Europe and a pickup in demand would first come next year.
Whether ABB will feel any boost from Europe this year is still unclear due to the uncertainties linked with the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) and the huge unemployment problem.
An increase in operating earnings came from improved results at the Power Generation, Financial Services, Power Transmission and Distribution segments and also transportation activities.
The only business segment that reported slightly lower results was at the Industrial and Building Systems segment, where the drop was due to sluggishness in Europe.
The 16 percent rise in first quarter orders was driven by large projects and increased demand from emerging markets, while orders for standard products and industrial goods were down.
The order backlog at the end of March amounted to $34.2 billion, up one percent from the end of the 1996 first quarter.
Additional orders from the Bakun, Malaysia, hydroelectric project were received in the first quarter, increasing orders at the Transmission and Distribution segment.
The Industrial and Building Systems segment also had higher orders, reflecting ABB's growing presence in oil, gas and petrochemical markets.
To help compensate for the weakness in Europe, Lindahl said ABB was increasing its sales efforts to increase market penetration and thus boost business volume.
"In our case we go for selective volume that can positively contribute to our bottom line," he said.
Another push is in the service and revamping business, where Lindahl said he still wants to double sales by year 2000 or 2001 from last year's $6 billion.
In both sales and service ABB is now increasing its staffing levels, Lindahl said, and this should "continue to give a good outcome in orders received."
